title: Fit a new hacksaw blade over both pins with its teeth pointing away from the handle, then tension it with the wing nut
instruction: Fit the new blade to the hacksaw.
context: Machinists, maintenance workers and fitters change hacksaw blades all the time (O*NET 49-9071.00, Maintenance and Repair Workers, General). A hacksaw cuts on the push stroke, so the blade goes on with its teeth pointing away from the handle, the way the arrow printed on every blade points, and its two holes over the frame's two pins. The wing nut is then run up until the blade is snug and turned one to two and a half turns more so the blade is taut. A blade fitted backwards cuts on the pull stroke, where it chatters, grabs and dulls its teeth; a slack blade flexes, wanders off the line and snaps in the cut, and an overtightened one tears at its holes. The fitter then lets go of the saw, which stays clamped in the vise ready for the next job.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A 12-inch hacksaw (red enameled steel channel frame, 2.2 cm deep and 1.2 cm thick, 10 cm throat, black pistol grip) lies flat with its frame 9 cm above the table, its back bar clamped along x 41 to 43 in a blue 4-inch bench vise (jaws centered at y 9.5, base 15 by 14 cm, fixed to the bench). The blade line runs along y at x 31. The two blade pins (3.5 mm steel, standing 7.5 mm up from steel spigots) are 30.48 cm apart at y -5.7 (front, nut end) and y 24.7 (rear, handle end). The front post carries an M6 tension screw along y; its cast steel wing nut (wings 4.6 cm tip to tip, 1 cm thick, 1.2 cm long, hub 1 cm) is at x 31, y -11.0, z 9.0, wings lying flat, backed off half a turn from snug. The rear post is at y 26.7 and the handle runs on to about y 40. The new blade, a 12-inch (30.5 cm between hole centers, 31.8 cm long) by 1.27 cm bi-metal blade, 0.65 mm thick with 18 teeth per inch, painted blue with three white arrows printed on each face pointing the way the teeth cut, lies across two hardwood blocks (4.5 by 4 by 3 cm, at x 18.0, y 0.9 and x 25.0, y 13.1). Its middle is at x 21.5, y 7.0, z 3.2; it lies askew at 30 degrees, its arrow pointing toward the handle's side (+y) and away from the robot, its teeth toward x+. Fitted correctly, the blade lies with its arrow pointing to -y (away from the handle) and its teeth facing the robot (away from the back bar): a 150 to 210 degree turn from where it starts. Both arms start at their ready pose. Real build: any 12-inch hacksaw frame with a front wing nut, a 4-inch bench vise and a 12-inch bi-metal blade; mount the vise so the frame sits 9 cm above the bench, and mark the blocks' footprints with tape.
scoring: The scorer watches the whole run. The blade is on both pins when each hole's center is within 3.25 mm of a pin's axis (the slot's 5 mm half-width less the pin's radius), its mid-plane within 2 mm of the seated height (a blade resting on a pin's top sits 7.5 mm high) and its face within 5 degrees of flat. Its teeth point the right way when the printed arrow is within 20 degrees of pointing away from the handle and the toothed edge within 20 degrees of facing away from the back bar. The wing nut's tension is its angle past snug, where the blade's slack is taken up; it starts half a turn short. Taut is 1 to 2.5 turns past snug (360 to 900 degrees): under one turn the blade still flexes sideways, and past 2.5 turns the pins start to tear its holes and the frame bows. Score 0 if the blade is not on both pins, if it points the wrong way (teeth toward the handle or toward the back bar), or if a gripper still holds the blade or the nut (fingers under 60 % open within 2 cm). 0.25 if the nut was never turned past snug. 0 if the nut went past snug while the blade was not on both pins (it was fitted to a tensioned frame, which a real saw does not allow; backing off to slack and refitting re-arms it), or if more than 90 degrees of its tightening was done without a gripper closed on its wings and rolling with them. Otherwise 0.5 if under one turn past snug, 0.25 if over 2.5 turns, and 1.0 between with both arms home and still (0.9 if not home). The overtight 0.25 sticks once the nut has gone past 2.5 turns with the blade on, even if it is backed off after, because torn holes stay torn; a blade knocked off the pins counts as off only after 10 steps in a row. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.9, 1. Real trial: check the arrow and that both pins show through the holes, count the wing nut's turns from snug with a paint mark on one wing, and check that nobody is holding the blade or the wing nut.
reset_notes: Back the wing nut off until the blade is slack and half a turn more, lift the blade off the pins and lay it across the two wooden blocks at its start pose (arrow toward the handle's side, 30 degrees askew). Nothing is used up; the same blade is reused.
fidelity: Everything is true size and the frame is fixed, as clamped. The blade is a rigid prop, 40 g (a real one is about 20 g), with a 3 mm collider so fingers can pinch its edges, and its holes are 10 mm slots in the collider (4 mm drawn), so a drop within 3.25 mm goes over the pins; a person seats a real 4 mm hole by feel. The thread is a model: the nut turns on a hinge with light resistance; tension is read from its angle, the blade and pins do not move.
